title: About This Site
text:
This is the course website for BEE 4850/5850, Environmental Data Analysis and Simulation, taught at Cornell University in the Department of Biological & Environmental Engineering in Spring 2027.
The site is built with Quarto, and the source is available on GitHub. Corrections and suggestions are welcome — use the “Edit this page” or “Report an issue” links in the right margin, or open an issue directly.

title: About This Site
text:
Credit
Course materials are by Vivek Srikrishnan unless otherwise noted, and are licensed CC-BY-SA 4.0. You are free to reuse and adapt them with attribution under the same license.
The site design derives from earlier offerings of this course and of BEE 4750/5750.
Several elements of the course’s structure are borrowed and adapted with thanks:

The four-step generative loop that organizes the course is adapted from Richard McElreath’s Statistical Rethinking (doi:10.1201/9780429029608), without its Bayesian commitment.
The homework assignment format — lettered sub-parts with individual point values, an agenda stating what is being practiced explicitly and implicitly, and instructions on the form of an answer — is adapted from Cosma Shalizi’s homework assignments for 36-401 and 36-402 at Carnegie Mellon.

title: Standard Rubrics
text: These rubrics are intended as a description for students and a guide to the grader for how to assign partial credit.

title: Standard Rubrics
text:
Meta-Rubric

Individual problems may vary from these standard rubrics based on the assessed learning outcomes for the problem, but they should give you an overview of what a solution ought to include.
Each bullet point appears as a separate rubric item in Gradescope. We use positive grading — points are awarded for each component, not deducted from a starting total.
Each standard rubric below describes partial credit for a 10-point problem. Partial credit for problems worth less should be scaled appropriately.
The graders cannot read your mind and will not try to. Submissions that are unclear for any reason — unclear syntax (English or code), uncommented code, missing reasoning, or so much detail that the argument is buried — will not be given credit. The grader has complete discretion here. If something in your solution is ambiguous, the grader has been instructed to interpret it the “wrong” way. Clear responses are a sign of understanding, which is part of what we are assessing.
You will not be doubly penalized for getting the “right” answer from the “wrong” setup, but this requires the grader to easily identify that your implementation is correct given your model.
You will not be given credit for your code. This is not a programming class; the code is a means to an end. Code that is sloppy but works is perfectly acceptable. However, clear code may earn you partial credit if the TA can easily see where a mistake crept in, so comment it and write down the mathematics of what it is meant to implement.
Some rubrics include deadly sins which cause an immediate zero for the problem. Do not do these.
Regardless of problem type, the following penalties apply per incident:

−1 for missing units;
−1 for an unlabeled figure axis;
−1 for reporting precision the data cannot support.

title: Standard Rubrics
text:
Standard Rubrics

Specifying a Model
10 points =

+4 for the specification. The distribution and link, written out, with the parameters named.
+4 for the assumptions. All of them — what is assumed about the errors, about independence, about the predictors. A specification missing its assumptions is not a specification.
+2 for the justification. Why that distribution? A constraint you are willing to state about the process, not “because it is standard.”







WarningDeadly Sin



Writing down a model with no assumptions stated at all. This is the single thing this course most wants you to stop doing, and it is an automatic zero for the problem.




Simulating From a Model
10 points =

+3 for the setup. What are you simulating, from which model, how many times, and why that many?
+4 for the implementation. Correct sampling from the specified model.
+3 for the interpretation. What did the simulation show, and what does it tell you about the model?



Fitting and Recovery
10 points =

+3 for the fit. Parameters reported with uncertainty, at sensible precision.
+4 for the recovery check. Simulate from the fit, refit, and compare. Did you get back what you put in?
+3 for the conclusion. If recovery failed, say so plainly and say what follows. A failed recovery honestly reported earns full credit here; a failed recovery not noticed earns none.



Model Comparison
10 points =

+3 for the criteria. Computed correctly, with the models clearly identified.
+4 for what each criterion is measuring. Predictive accuracy or marginal likelihood? This is the point of the exercise.
+3 for the recommendation. Which model, why, and what result would change your mind.







WarningDeadly Sin



Reporting that AIC and BIC disagree and stopping there. Disagreement is the beginning of the answer — explain what the disagreement tells you about the models.




Interpretation Questions
10 points =

+5 for the claim. A direct answer to the question asked.
+5 for the reasoning. Why, in terms of the actual variables and the actual model — not in terms of “the predictor variable” or “X.”







ImportantDon’t Bullshit



You will get no points for word salad, even if you accidentally hit on the right answer. A short, correct, clearly-reasoned paragraph beats a page of hedging every time.

title: Quiz Policies
text: This page includes information on the quizzes for BEE 4850/5850, including policies and logistics.

title: Quiz Policies
text:
Quiz Logistics
There are six quizzes, given in class, taking approximately the first 25 minutes of the session. Quizzes will be hand-written and then scanned into Gradescope (by course staff) for grading and feedback; the physical copy will not be returned.
The dates and what each quiz covers are on the quiz schedule.
Together the quizzes are worth 25% of your grade. The lowest quiz is dropped, for students in both 4850 and 5850.






ImportantA Quiz Never Covers The Same Week



Every quiz covers material through the previous Friday at the latest, and nothing after it. This is a rule, not a tendency, and it is why the quiz dates sit where they do. It also guarantees there is always a homework assignment covering the material, returned to you, before the quiz that tests it.

title: Quiz Policies
text:
Quiz Topics and Structure
The emphasis is on concepts. There is no programming, and there are no formulas requiring memorization. Expect 3–5 questions worth 1–3 points each, drawn from the same six forms the homework assignments rehearse:

State the model with its assumptions — write out the equations, including any and all assumptions;
Define a property — what does it mean for an estimator to be unbiased?
Read a diagnostic — here is an ACF, a trace plot, a residual plot: what does it tell you?
Interpret a result — often as true/false statements about a reported interval;
Small computation — how many Monte Carlo samples for a given standard error?
State an assumption — what does the non-parametric bootstrap assume?

In general, the same grading rubric applies to quiz problems as appropriate (e.g. nothing about code). Your solutions should be clear, with transparent and well-communicated reasoning.

Difficulty
Quiz problems are closer in difficulty to homework assignment problems than to mini project problems, since you have weeks to work on a mini project with full access to external resources, course staff, and classmates. The goal is to assess your ability to understand concepts, set up problems, determine the appropriateness of methods, and interpret output — not to do computations under time pressure. We cannot, and do not, expect you to solve mini-project-level problems in a 25-minute closed-book setting.
The homework assignments are the sample quizzes. That is what they are for, and it is why there is one before every quiz.

title: Quiz Policies
text:
Academic Integrity
Quizzes are closed-book, closed-note, and closed-everything else. No medically unnecessary electronic devices are allowed, including headphones and smart watches.
Quizzes are strictly confidential until all conflict and accommodation quizzes have been taken. Do not discuss a quiz with anyone, in person or online, until we have discussed it in class.

title: Quiz Policies
text:
Accommodations, Conflicts, and Makeups

SDS Accommodations
Please make sure that any exam-related accommodations have been provided to the course staff ahead of the first quiz. Quizzes requiring accommodations will be scheduled and delivered through the Alternative Testing Program.


Conflicts and Makeups
If you have an academic conflict or a university-approved reason why you cannot take a quiz in class, contact Prof. Srikrishnan ahead of the quiz to arrange an alternative.
Because the lowest quiz is dropped, a single missed quiz for an unforeseeable reason generally needs no further accommodation — the drop absorbs it. In extreme circumstances, such as long-term illness or injury preventing more than one quiz, we may forgive additional quizzes and compute your grade without them. This will dramatically increase the weight given to other assessments.

title: Homework Policies
text:
What Homework Are For
Previous offerings of this course had a problem, and it was mine, not yours. You were assessed with 25-minute closed-book quizzes asking you to write out a model, define a property, or read a diagnostic plot. The only practice you got was homework — but homework then meant a two-week computational assignment, where you had a laptop, the internet, your classmates, and fourteen days. Those measure different things, and only one of them was being practiced.
So homework in this course is a different animal from what that word used to mean here: nine short assignments rather than five long ones, mostly on paper, in the format the quiz actually uses.
Homework close that gap. They are in the quiz’s exact idiom — same question forms, same expectation of a written answer, same absence of a computer for most of it — at about 1.3 times a quiz’s length. If you can do the homework assignment, you can do the quiz. That is the entire design.






ImportantThe Practice Is The Point, Not The Score



A homework assignment is worth about 2% of your course grade. It is not there to sort you; it is there to tell you — before the quiz, while it is still free — whether you can actually write out a null model or read an ACF. If you look at the key before attempting the problems, you will get the satisfying feeling of understanding and none of the actual understanding. I have seen this go wrong many times, and it always goes wrong the same way.

NoteA Homework Point Is Not A Quiz Point



A homework assignment is 20 points and about 45 minutes. A quiz is 6 points and 25 minutes. A homework point is therefore worth roughly half a quiz point — homework is open-book, untimed, and scored at finer granularity, so a point buys less. Do not read “20 points” as three quizzes’ worth of work. If an assignment is taking you dramatically longer than 45 minutes, that is useful information and I would like to hear about it.

title: Homework Policies
text:
Logistics

Homework are due at 9:00pm Eastern on the due date, which is always a Friday. Submit to Gradescope as a PDF with pages tagged. Failure to tag pages results in a non-negotiable 10% deduction.
Late submissions are accepted up to 24 hours, at full credit.
The solution key posts when the late window closes, one day after the deadline. No submissions are accepted after the key is public.
The lowest homework assignment is dropped automatically.
Collaboration is encouraged. Write up your own answers in your own words, and list who you worked with.

title: Homework Policies
text:
How They Are Marked
Every question is checked against the posted key. Two or three questions per assignment additionally receive written feedback.
Why the difference? Because a posted key and a grader do different jobs. If you defined the logit incorrectly or got the sample-size calculation wrong, the key tells you that, and a paragraph from the TA adds nothing. What a key cannot catch is reasoning that is plausible and wrong — and that is exactly what happens on questions like “why can two defensible null models give different p-values?” Those answers can read perfectly well and be wrong, and only a human notices. So written feedback goes where the key is insufficient.
Which questions get written feedback varies from week to week and is not announced in advance. This is deliberate: if you knew, you would optimize for those two questions, which defeats the purpose.






WarningThe Computational Item Counts



Problem 3 is not optional garnish. An assignment submitted without a serious attempt at all three problems, including the computational one, does not receive credit — it is not marked out of 14.
This is the only thing in the course keeping your hands on a keyboard between mini projects, and the wrangling it asks for (grouping, joining, handling gaps) is a skill this course expects you to build through practice rather than lecture.

title: Homework Policies
text:
Answers, Not Output
For the computational item specifically:

Answer in sentences. Raw program output pasted into a PDF is not an answer to anything.
Label your figures. Axis labels with units, a legend if there is more than one thing plotted. A figure that needs you standing next to it to explain is not doing its job.
Avoid excessive precision. If you report a return level as 3.847261 m, you are claiming something about the sixth decimal place that your 40 years of data cannot support.

title: Environmental Data Analysis and Simulation
text:
What This Course Is About
Statistics are not magic.
A t-test is not a black box that emits a p-value — it is a model of what your data would look like if nothing were going on, and you can build that model yourself. Once you can build that one, you can build the one that actually fits your problem, which is usually not the one in the textbook.
That is the whole course. Every method we meet gets run through the same four steps:

Why that distribution and link?
Simulate from the model you specified.
Fit it to data.
Test — did you get back what you put in?

Step 4 is where the learning happens, and it is the step most often skipped. We will not skip it.

ImportantThe Proposal Is Where Problem Formulation Gets Assessed

The proposal lands after MP1 is returned, so you know what a full pass through the loop actually costs before you promise one — and before spring break, so feedback reaches you with time to change course.

title: Grading Policies
text:
How Work Is Graded

Homework is graded by the TA on Gradescope. Every question is checked against the posted solution key; two or three questions per assignment additionally receive written feedback. See Homework Policies for why the depth varies.
Quizzes are graded by Prof. Srikrishnan and the TA using the same principles as the homework assignment key. These are scanned and graded on Gradescope.
Mini projects are graded by Prof. Srikrishnan using the rubrics.
Term projects are graded by Prof. Srikrishnan. The proposal is graded substantively, not for completeness — it is the only place in this course where problem formulation is assessed. The check-in is pass/fail.

title: Grading Policies
text:
Late Policies and Extension Requests

Homework can be submitted up to 24 hours late for full credit. The solution key is posted when that window closes, and no submissions are accepted after that point. The lowest homework assignment is dropped.
Mini projects and project deliverables can be submitted up to 24 hours late for 50% credit. Submissions after 24 hours will not be accepted unless an extension was granted (in which case there is no late penalty until the extension date). This lets us release solutions and return grades ASAP.
Request extensions ahead of the deadline. Justified extensions will only be granted for university-approved reasons or emergencies such as illness, injury, learning accommodations, etc., and will be limited to 1-2 days depending on the circumstance. Deadlines in other courses, job interviews, etc. are not reasons for extensions. Ask yourself whether the circumstances leading to your extension request interfered with submission due to poor planning or because they rendered you incapable of work and/or submission. Extensions requested after the deadline will only be considered prior to solution release and for extreme circumstances (e.g. hospitalization during the last day, hence limited communication access).
Under extreme circumstances, we will forgive assignments. There are circumstances under which a 24 hour extension is insufficient, such as long-term illness or serious injury. In these cases, we will compute your course grade as if the forgiven assignment never occurred, which will result in your other assessments having more weight.







ImportantThe Drops Are There To Be Used



One homework assignment, one quiz, and one reading are dropped automatically. That is not slack for you to plan around — it is insurance for the week when something goes wrong. If you burn all three in February because you were busy, and then get sick in April, we are both in a worse position than if you had come to talk to me.

title: Grading Policies
text:
Regrade Requests

Submit regrade requests on Gradescope within one week of the grade release. We recommend talking to Prof. Srikrishnan or your TA about grading concerns before submitting a regrade request, but no grades will be changed outside of a formal request through Gradescope.
All regrade requests must include a brief justification for the request or they will not be considered. Good justifications include (but are not limited to):

My answer agrees with the posted solution, but I still lost points.
I lost 4 points for something, but the rubric says it should only be worth 2 points.
You took points off for something, but it’s right here.
My answer is correct, even though it does not match the posted solution.
There is no explanation for my grade.
I got a perfect score, but my solution has a mistake (you will receive extra credit for this! see below!)
There is a major error in the posted solution; here is an explanation (full credit for everyone, but Prof. Srikrishnan will decide what constitutes a “major error”! see below!).

We will only regrade what you submitted. Any “new” information in the regrade request will not be considered beyond the justification. An explanation may help us identify where to look if your solution is different than the official solution but correct, but the submitted answer must be interpretable as a correct solution on its own merits.
The first regrade request will be handled by the member of the course staff who graded the problem. If Prof. Srikrishnan did not review the first request, he will handle any subsequent regrade requests for the same submission. Once Prof. Srikrishnan issues a response to a regrade request, further requests for that submission will be ignored.
If you submit a regrade request correctly reporting that your problem was graded too leniently, your score will be increased by the difference (we want to reward this type of honesty and self-awareness!). For example, if your score was 8/10, and you point out that you should have gotten a 3/10, your score will be a 13/10.
If a significant error is found in the official solutions, everyone in the class will receive full credit for the relevant (sub)problem. Prof. Srikrishnan has discretion as to what errors are “significant.”

title: Mini Project and Term Project Policies
text:
Mini Projects
There are two mini projects, each computational and unit-scale. Together they are worth 20% of your grade.
Dates are on the project schedule.
These may be completed individually or in pairs. See Group Work for expectations if you work in a pair.

Accepting and Submitting

Mini projects are distributed through GitHub Classroom. When one is released, a link to accept it will be posted on Ed Discussion. You must click this link or subsequent steps will not work properly. Clicking it creates your own repository with the assignment files.
Clone your repository, not the original template.
Open the local repository folder (use File -> Open Folder, not File -> Open) so that all paths point to the right location.
Run the initial notebook cell (starting with Pkg.activate()) to load the Julia environment and install packages.
Commit and push frequently. This helps us answer questions, and gives you a backstop if something goes wrong close to the deadline — the timestamp of your commit is evidence that you finished on time even if we cannot render your PDF until the next day.
Submit a PDF to Gradescope with pages tagged. Failure to tag pages results in a non-negotiable 10% deduction.
Due at 9:00pm Eastern. Late submissions accepted within 24 hours at a 50% penalty.



What We Are Looking For
Both mini projects are a full pass through the loop, and both are graded against the rubrics. MP1 is deliberately incomplete in ways later weeks expose — Gaussian errors that maximum entropy will question, residual independence that the time series week will test. That is not a flaw in the assignment; we will come back to it in lecture, and noticing it yourself is worth saying out loud in your writeup.






NoteMP2 Has Gaps In It, On Purpose



The record you are given for MP2 has missing months, because real gauge records do. Computing an annual maximum from a year with a three-month gap is a genuine open problem, not an exercise — is that year’s maximum real, or an artifact of what was not recorded? Missing-data mechanisms are covered in lecture during MP2’s window, which is deliberate. Say what you did about the gaps and why.




BEE 5850 Requirements

MP1: the Bayesian treatment is required, not an optional extension.
MP2: WAIC must be computed from your own posterior, not from the provided posterior sample.

title: Mini Project and Term Project Policies
text:
Term Project
The term project is 25% of your grade, and is a question and dataset of your own choosing. It may be completed individually or in pairs.
There are three deliverables — a proposal, a check-in, and a report with presentation. Dates are on the project schedule.

The Proposal
No more than 2 pages (11 point font, 1 inch margins), not including figures or references, covering:

The underlying science question and any associated hypotheses;
The dataset(s) you will analyze;
Statistical model(s) for the hypotheses and your planned strategy for analysis.







ImportantThis Is Where Problem Formulation Gets Assessed



The proposal is the only place in this course where you decide what question is worth asking of what data. Everywhere else, I hand you the problem. It is graded accordingly — substantively, not as an administrative step.
The test I will apply: can you say what would count as an answer? A proposal that cannot does not yet describe a project, however interesting the dataset. Come talk to me early if you are not sure.




The Check-In
A ten-minute conversation in office hours, not a written deliverable. Pass/fail on having something to show. Its job is to catch a project going wrong while there is still time to fix it, which a conversation does better than a document.


The Report
No more than 5 pages (11 point font, 1 inch margins), not including references and figures. Detailed rubrics will be provided later in the semester.
Every report must include a section stating what a conventional canned analysis of your data would have concluded, and why yours differs. If it does not differ, say so and explain why — that is a legitimate finding, and sometimes the standard analysis is the right one. What is not acceptable is not knowing.


BEE 5850 Requirements
Students in BEE 5850 must additionally defend their specification against a named alternative specification, including a simulation study establishing the conditions under which the two diverge and what evidence would distinguish them. “I chose a GEV” is a specification; “I chose a GEV rather than a GPD, and here is the sample size at which that choice stops mattering” is a defense.


Presentations
Presentations run during the university finals period, at a date and time assigned by the Office of the University Registrar. Expect to devote approximately 6 hours to the project during the exam period.

title: Group Expectations
Group Expectations
Group Expectations
Academic Integrity
text: While we don’t expect academic integrity to be a problem (we trust you, which is why the course is designed to be open and collaborative!), these policy statements are unfortunately necessary due to a very small minority of students. If you are worried about whether something you are doing is in danger of violating this course’s academic integrity policy, please don’t hesitate to ask during lecture, in office hours, by email, or on Ed Discussion.

title: Academic Integrity
text:
Expectations






ImportantOur Expectations



Each student or group must write their own solutions in their own words and submit work that reflects their understanding. All external sources, including classmates, must be properly credited and referenced.**


If something is submitted with your name on it, you should be able to explain and defend its choices and outcomes. This is true in the workplace as well as in academia.
For example, see:

The Cornell University Code of Academic Integrity;
The American Society for Civil Engineers’ Code of Ethics.

This issue is particularly important in engineering, as lives and well-being depend on the honesty and integrity of engineers. While the stakes are obviously lower in our class, the habits you develop now are related to your practices in the future.

Cite Your Sources and Collaborators
This course is designed to be highly collaborative: you are free to work with classmates, seek out their advice and insights when you are stuck, and provide help to them when they are stuck. You are also highly encouraged to take advantage of external resources to help you solve problems. But you must cite your sources, with only three exceptions:

Help from the instructor or course staff;
Course materials from this semester;
Sources used in prerequisite courses.

Submitting someone else’s work or ideas without proper credit is plagiarism, even if you have their permission. Plagiarism, and facilitating plagiarism, are academic integrity violations and will be treated accordingly. Conversely, citing your sources will never negatively impact your grade, and may help if you relied on poor information which you then used properly.


Use Your Own Words
Duplication of any source, even with proper citation, is plagiarism. Your submissions must reflect your own ideas, understanding, and work. This means:

Verbatim copying of lecture notes (including code samples) is plagiarism;
Copying from old homework assignment, mini project, or quiz solutions is plagiarism;
Submitting work in your name done by another student is plagiarism;
Allowing another student is submit your work in their name is an academic integrity violation.
Minor wordsmithing to change individual words while preserving a duplicated text’s flow of ideas is also an academic integrity violation. For example, taking ChatGPT output and copying it is clearly an academic integrity violation; changing a few words here or there to avoid “duplication” is still a violation.

This also goes for any code that you submit. While you are welcome to draw on sources such as ChatGPT or Stack Overflow for debugging, syntax help, or programming patterns, you should independently incorporate these ideas into your independently written problem solutions and code (and credit them in the comments!). If the instructor or TA ask you to explain what is going on in your code, and you cannot, there’s a problem.

title: Academic Integrity
Academic Integrity
text:
Penalties

If you commit an academic integrity violation on a homework assignment or mini project, you will be given a zero for that entire assignment, which will not be dropped under any circumstances.
If you commit an academic integrity violation on a quiz, you will be given a zero for that entire quiz, which will not be dropped under any circumstances.
If you commit a second academic integrity violation, you will be given an F for the course.
If your first violation is particularly egregious, you will be given an F for the course.

All academic integrity violations will also be reported to the students’ college and department.

title: Academic Integrity
text:
Group Work
Your term project involves the submission of work jointly as a group. This means that every member of the group is responsible for the entire project. At a minimum, every person whose name is on a submission must read, understand, and approve the entirety of the submission (this is the same standard used for authorship on academic publications). Allowing someone else to add your name to something you did not contribute to is an academic integrity violation and will result in a zero for the entire submission.

title: Academic Integrity
section: A Note On LLMs Specific To This Course
text:
A Note On LLMs Specific To This Course
The AI/ML policy above applies: use these tools if you find them useful, and disclose it when you do.
But there is a failure mode particular to this material that is worth naming. Large language models are very good at producing statistical analysis that looks right — a plausible model, a confident justification, a clean figure — and that is precisely the thing this course exists to teach you to detect. The whole argument of this class is that you cannot tell whether an analysis is any good by looking at whether it reads well; you have to ask what generative model it assumes, what it checked, and what it took on faith.
So if you use one of these tools and cannot answer why that distribution, why that link, and why that null model, you have not done the assignment, whatever is on the page. You will also discover this on a quiz, where the tool is not available and 25 minutes is not long enough to develop an understanding you never had.

The emphasis is on concepts. There is no programming, and nothing requiring memorized formulas. Expect 3–5 questions worth 1–3 points each, drawn from the same six forms the homework assignments rehearse:

title: Syllabus
text:
This is a 3 credit course offered as an elective.





 Vivek Srikrishnan
 vs498@cornell.edu
 318 Riley-Robb Hall






 TBD
 TBD
 TBD






 MWF
 11:15-12:05
 401 Riley-Robb Hall






Understanding data is an increasingly integral part of working with environmental systems. Data analysis is a critical part of understanding system dynamics and projecting future conditions and outcomes. This course provides an overview of a generative approach to environmental data analysis: instead of treating statistical methods as a menu of named procedures to be looked up and applied, we treat every analysis as a model of how the data came to be, which we can write down, simulate from, fit, and test.
That framing is the spine of the course, and we will run the same four-step loop on every model we meet:

Why that distribution and link? What constraints are you willing to state about the process, and what distribution do those constraints imply?
Simulate. Generate data from the model you just specified.
Fit. Estimate the parameters from data, by maximum likelihood or from a posterior.
Test. Did you get back what you put in? What does the model fail to reproduce?

Step 4 is where most of the learning happens, and it is the step most often skipped in practice. We will not skip it.
In particular, over the course of the semester, we will:

conduct exploratory analyses and build visualizations of environmental datasets;
recover familiar named statistical tests by building their null models from scratch and simulating from them;
specify generative models for environmental data, justifying the distribution and link from stated constraints;
quantify and propagate uncertainty using Monte Carlo, the bootstrap, and Bayesian inference;
compare competing models on evidence, and say what each criterion is actually measuring;
apply all of this where it is hardest, on extreme values and on data with gaps.

title: Syllabus
section: What Should You Leave This Course With
text:
What Should You Leave This Course With
Statistics should not be a black box. If there is one thing I want you to leave this course with, it is this. A t-test is not a black box that emits a p-value; it is a model of how your data would look if nothing were going on, and you can build that model yourself. Once you can, you can also build the one that fits your problem, which is usually not the one in the textbook or software package.

Prerequisites & Preparation
The following courses/material would be ideal preparation:

One course in programming (e.g. CS 1110, 1112 or ENGRD/CEE 3200)
One course in probability or statistics (ENGRD 2700, CEE 3040, or equivalent)

In the absence of one or more these prerequisites, you can seek the permission of instructor.

If your programming or statistics skills are a little rusty, don’t worry! We will review concepts and build skills as needed. Weeks 1–2 are deliberately a re-grounding in probability and simulation before anything new gets built on top of them.

McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan, 2nd ed. Chapman and Hall/CRC. doi:10.1201/9780429029608. This is where the four-step loop and the maximum-entropy justification for distribution choice come from. title: Syllabus
text:
Community

Diversity and Inclusion
Our goal is for this class to be a learning environment in which everyone can participate fully. Diversity of background and perspective makes for better engineering and better science, and I want the classroom to reflect that. If anything — in the material, in how the class is run, or in how people treat each other — is making that harder for you, please tell me.






ImportantPlease, Be Excellent To Each Other



Treat your classmates and the course staff with respect, in class, in office hours, and on Ed Discussion. Disagreement about statistics is welcome and encouraged; dismissiveness toward a classmate who is still working something out is not.




Student Accommodations
If you have a disability-related need for accommodations in this class, please get an accommodation letter from Student Disability Services and speak with me as early in the semester as possible so we can put arrangements in place. Accommodations cannot be applied retroactively, so earlier is genuinely better.
If you experience a short-term disability or an injury during the semester, let me know and we will work something out.


Course Communications
Use Ed Discussion for all class-related questions. This is not because I don’t want to hear from you — it is because a question you have is almost always a question somebody else has, and answering it in one place helps everybody. Reserve email for matters that are genuinely private (accommodations, personal circumstances, grades).






TipEd Tips




Search before posting; there’s a decent chance your question has been asked.
Post questions publicly unless there’s a reason not to. You can post anonymously to your classmates if you prefer.
If you’re asking about code, link to the relevant file and line in your GitHub repository rather than pasting a large block.
Answer each other’s questions! This is encouraged and is a good way to check whether you actually understand something.





Mental Health Resources
Your wellbeing matters more than this class does. If you are struggling, please reach out — to me, to your advisor, or to Cornell Health (607-255-5155). Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) offers same-day appointments, and Cornell’s crisis resources are available 24/7.






ImportantMental Health And This Class



If something is going on that is getting in the way of your work in this course, tell me early, and in general terms if you prefer — you do not owe me any details. The course has a dropped homework assignment, a dropped quiz, and a dropped reading built into it precisely so that a bad week costs you nothing. Those are there to be used. What I cannot easily fix is a problem I hear about for the first time in May.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Policies
More detail on all of these is on the course policies pages.

Attendance
Attendance is not graded, but quizzes are given in class and cannot be made up outside of the university’s accommodation processes. If you must miss class, get notes from a classmate and come to office hours with specific questions.






TipWhat If I’m Sick?



Please stay home. Genuinely — do not come to class sick. Contact me as soon as you can if you will miss a quiz, and we will use the drop or, if it comes to that, forgive the quiz and reweight.




Academic Integrity
Cornell’s Academic Integrity Code applies to all work in this class.
In practice, for this course:

Homework and mini projects: collaboration is encouraged. Write up your own solution, in your own words, and list everyone you worked with.
Quizzes: closed-book, closed-note, closed-everything. No collaboration of any kind.
Term project: your own work (or your pair’s), with all sources cited.
Cite every outside source you use, including AI tools — see the AI/ML resource policy.







WarningWhy Can’t I Consult Old Solutions?



Solutions from previous offerings of this course, or solutions circulating online, are off limits. This is partly an integrity matter, but mostly a practical one: the point of a homework assignment is the attempt, and reading a solution before attempting it destroys the thing the assignment is for. You will feel like you understood it, sit a quiz, and discover that you didn’t. I have watched this happen many times.




AI/ML Resource Policy
You may use LLMs and similar tools, and you must disclose it when you do — describe what you asked and how you used the output. See the integrity policy for the full version.
A warning specific to this course: these tools are quite good at producing statistical analysis that looks right but is not based on clear and transparent reasoning.


Office Hours
Office hours are listed on the course home page. They are for whatever you need them for — questions on the material, help getting unstuck on an assignment, or talking through your project.






TipWhat If I Can’t Make Office Hours?



Post on Ed Discussion, or email me to set up another time. If the scheduled hours don’t work for a large number of you, tell me and I will move them.

Technologies
We will use Canvas as a gradebook and to distribute PDFs of readings (also made available through the website when possible, via the Cornell library). Ed Discussion will be used for course communications. Assignments will be submitted and graded in Gradescope. Mini projects will be distributed through GitHub Classroom.
Students can use any programming language they like to solve problems, though we will make notebooks and package environments available for Julia (which may help structure your assignments if you use a different language) via GitHub. If students use a language other than Julia, we may be limited in the programming assistance we can provide (though we’re happy to try to help!).
We recommend students create a GitHub account and use GitHub to version control and share their code throughout the semester.

Homework
There will be nine homework assignments over the semester, each worth 20 points. These are pen-and-paper, in the same idiom as the quizzes, plus one short computational item. Expect each to take about 45 minutes: roughly 30 minutes of written work and 15 minutes at the keyboard.
Homework exist for one reason: to rehearse the quiz. Previous offerings of this course assessed you with 25-minute closed-book quizzes while the only practice was two-week computational homework. Those measure different things, and only one of them was being practiced. The homework assignments fix that.
Each assignment has three problems:

Problem 1 (7 points) — a short scenario with three sub-parts, walking through the loop on one object;
Problem 2 (7 points) — three standalone short questions, exactly in the quiz’s format;
Problem 3 (6 points) — the computational item, ending in a figure and a sentence of interpretation.

Some notes on homework logistics:

Homework are due at 9:00pm Eastern on the due date (always a Friday). Submit to Gradescope as a PDF with pages tagged.
Late work is accepted up to one day late, and the solution key is posted when that window closes — see the callout below.
The lowest homework assignment is dropped automatically.
Every question is checked against the posted key, and two or three questions per assignment receive written feedback. Which questions get written feedback varies from week to week and is not announced in advance.
The computational item counts. An assignment submitted without a serious attempt at all three problems, including the computational one, will not receive credit.







ImportantWhy The Key Goes Up A Day After The Deadline



The solution key for each homework assignment is posted when the late window closes, not when the assignment is due. This is so that a one-day-late submission isn’t just a copy of the key.
It also means the key is always in your hands well before the quiz it rehearses — at minimum two days, usually six or more. Written feedback on the marked questions may arrive after the quiz, and that’s fine: the forms of question recur across all six quizzes, so feedback on how you stated a model in February is still useful in April.




Quizzes
Quizzes will be given in class at the end of several units. These will be in the first half of the relevant class, approximately 25 minutes long. No materials (books, notes, computers, or calculators) are allowed. Quizzes will be scanned into Gradescope for grading.
There are six quizzes, and the lowest is dropped, for students in both 4850 and 5850. The material covered will be specified ahead of time in class and on Ed Discussion. As a rule, a quiz never covers material from the same week it is given — every quiz covers through the previous Friday at the latest.
The emphasis is on concepts. There is no programming on a quiz and nothing requiring memorized formulas. You will be asked to write out models and their assumptions, define properties, read diagnostic plots, interpret results, and do small calculations — which is exactly what the homework assignments rehearse.


Readings
Readings will be assigned throughout the semester to help you engage with the background and the uses of the material for that week. There are 8 required readings, provided as PDFs on Canvas through Perusall and (when possible through open access or the Cornell library) linked from the website.
Students are expected to demonstrate engagement through collaborative annotations — your own comments on parts you found interesting or had questions about, or responses to other students’ annotations. You should also post an overall reflection, synthesizing your takeaways with content from this or other classes, on Ed Discussion. Both should be completed by the start of the first lecture the next week. You are not graded on the quantity of annotations, but on the degree to which they reflect critical engagement. One reading assignment will be dropped automatically.
Four questions are worth asking of every reading, and they are the same four all semester:

What generative model did the authors assume?
What did they simulate, and what did they take on faith?
How did they check the model?
What would you have checked that they did not?

All students write one discussion paper late in the semester applying these four questions at length:

BEE 4850: a one-page analysis of a paper of your choosing or one from the pool.
BEE 5850: a full referee report, 2–3 pages, written to the standard a journal would expect, including a recommendation (accept / minor revision / major revision / reject) and the reasoning behind it. Discuss your choice of paper with me to make sure it is appropriate.



Mini Projects
There are two mini projects, each computational and unit-scale, distributed through GitHub Classroom. These may be completed individually or in pairs.

Mini Project 1 — Regression and Simulation. Assigned Monday, March 1; due Wednesday, March 17. Specify a linear generative model for an environmental dataset, simulate from it, fit it, check whether you recover what you put in, and put uncertainty on the fit with the bootstrap. For 5850, the Bayesian treatment is required; for 4850 it is an optional extension.
Mini Project 2 — Extremes, with Model Comparison. Assigned Monday, April 5; due Friday, May 7. Fit a GEV and a GPD to a real record, fit stationary and nonstationary variants, and compare them on evidence — cross-validation where defensible, plus WAIC, AIC, and BIC — saying explicitly what each is measuring and why they may disagree. For 5850, WAIC must be computed from your own posterior rather than a provided sample.







NoteMP2 Has Gaps In It, On Purpose



The record you are given for MP2 has missing months, because real gauge records do. Computing an annual maximum from a year with a three-month gap is a genuine open problem, not an exercise — is that year’s maximum real, or an artifact of what wasn’t recorded? Missing-data mechanisms are covered in lecture during MP2’s window, which is deliberate.




Term Project
Throughout the semester, students will apply the concepts and methods from class to a question and data set of their own choosing. If you do not have a data set in mind, come talk to me and we will find one that aligns with your interests.
The term project can be completed individually or in groups of 2. There are three deliverables:

A proposal (no more than 2 pages, 11 point font, 1 inch margins, not including figures or references), due Friday, March 26, including:

The underlying science question for your project and any associated hypotheses;
The dataset(s) you will analyze and use to test your hypotheses;
Statistical model(s) for the hypotheses and your planned strategy for analysis.

A check-in, due Friday, April 23. This is a ten-minute conversation in office hours rather than a written deliverable, graded pass/fail on having something to show.
A final report, due during the finals period. No more than 5 pages (11 point font, 1 inch margins), not including references and figures. More details and rubrics will be provided later in the semester.

The report must include a section stating what a conventional canned analysis of your data would have concluded, and why yours differs. If it doesn’t differ, say so and explain why — that is a legitimate finding, and sometimes the standard analysis is the right one.
Students in BEE 5850 must additionally defend their specification against a named alternative specification, including a simulation study establishing the conditions under which the two diverge and what evidence would distinguish them.






ImportantThe Proposal Is Where Problem Formulation Gets Assessed



It is the only place in this course where you decide what question is worth asking of what data, and it is weighted accordingly rather than treated as an administrative step. A proposal that cannot say what would count as an answer does not yet describe a project. Start thinking about this well before March.


Presentations will be held during the university finals period, at a date and time assigned by the Office of the University Registrar. In addition to work completed during the semester, students can expect to devote approximately 6 hours to the term project during the exam period.


Late Work Policy
Homework may be submitted up to 24 hours late for full credit, after which the solution key is posted and no further submissions can be accepted. The lowest homework assignment is dropped.
Mini projects and project deliverables may be submitted up to 24 hours late at a 50% penalty, and will not be accepted after that point. This policy may seem strict, but allows for prompt release of solutions and discussion of assignments. Please reach out as soon as possible (ideally before the due date) if legitimate circumstances emerge which prevent you from submitting work on time; we will make accommodations for approved reasons, which might include a limited extension or forgiving the assignment.


Regrade Requests
Regrade requests can be submitted up to one week after the graded work is released on Gradescope.
All regrade requests must include a brief justification for the request or they will not be considered. Good justifications include (but are not limited to):

My answer agrees with the posted solution, but I still lost points.
I lost 4 points for something, but the rubric says it should only be worth 2 points.
You took points off for something, but it’s right here.
My answer is correct, even though it does not match the posted solution; here is an explanation.
There is no explanation for my grade.
I got a perfect score, but my solution has a mistake (you will receive extra credit for this! see below!)
There is a major error in the posted solution; here is an explanation (full credit for everyone, but Prof. Srikrishnan will decide what constitutes a “major error”! see below!).







ImportantWe Can Only Grade What You Submitted



All regrades will be assessed based only on the submitted work. You cannot get a higher grade by explaining what you meant (either in person or online) or by adding information or reasoning to what is submitted after the fact. The goal of the regrade is to draw attention to a potential grading problem, not to supplement the submission.


The first regrade request for any submission will be handled by the person who graded that problem. If the submission was graded by the TA, additional regrade requests for the same submission will be handled directly by the instructor. Once Prof. Srikrishnan issues a final response to a regrade request, further requests for that submission will be ignored.






WarningRegrade Requests Can Be A Gamble!



While you should submit regrade requests for legitimate errors, using them for fishing expeditions can also result in lost points if the TA or Prof. Srikrishnan decide that your initial grade was too lenient or if additional errors are identified.








TipWhat If I Find A Different Type of Mistake?




If you submit a regrade request correctly reporting that a problem was graded too leniently — that is, that your score was higher than it should be based on the rubric — your score will be increased by the difference. For example, if your original score on a problem was 8/10 and you successfully argue that your score should have been 3/10, your new score will be 13/10. However, don’t fish — your grade might be lowered if the TA finds an independent mistake while regrading.
If a significant error is discovered in a posted solution, everyone in the class will receive full credit for the (sub)problem. Prof. Srikrishnan will decide what is “significant”.
